title: Toward Effective and Reliable LLM Agents via Dynamic Ontology
thesis: Ontology can act as a kernel for agents: task-oriented ontologies and knowledge graphs are constructed dynamically and refined using judge feedback (OaK).
mechanism: Dynamic construction of task-oriented ontology/KG, iterative refinement driven by judge feedback.
evidence: Datasets, baselines, metrics and quantitative results not recovered in this session.
limitations: Unverified: evaluation scope, cost of judge loop, drift of refined ontology. Full text not read.
implications: Closest external analogue to World0 dynamic concept/relation evolution. Judge-feedback refinement could drive relation retyping and card merging. Risk: task-oriented ontologies may be too narrow versus World0's context-sensitive projection of one shared structure.

claims: An ontology built and refined per task (ontology-as-kernel) makes LLM agents more effective and reliable.
premises: Agent failures are partly caused by missing or unstable task structure.
Judge feedback is informative enough to refine an ontology.
counterpoints: Per-task ontologies may fragment knowledge across tasks; World0 instead keeps one shared structure and projects it per context.
Cost of a judge loop per task is unknown.
interpretation: Feedback-driven refinement is the transferable idea, not per-task ontologies.

title: Remember Before You're Asked: MemDream for Self-Probing Memory Evolution
thesis: Memory should be repaired offline before retrieval fails, via self-probing dream cycles.
mechanism: Offline dream cycles with three agents (Dreamer, Analyst, Consolidator) that probe, diagnose and repair a memory graph; policy trained with GRPO; soft decay gives reversible forgetting; online interaction continues during consolidation.
evidence: Numerical results not recovered in this session.
limitations: Unverified: benchmark coverage, RL training cost, whether repairs introduce semantic drift.
implications: Maps directly onto a World0 Dream Mechanism: probe the concept-world with synthetic task contexts, diagnose weak projections, repair relations. Reversible decay matches the 'never silently delete' stance. Complexity: medium-high; start with a non-RL probe/diagnose/repair loop using the existing projection eval scripts.

claims: Repairing a memory graph offline, before retrieval fails, improves long-term agent memory.
premises: Memory failures are detectable by self-probing before a user query exposes them.
A learned policy (GRPO) can prioritize what to probe and repair.
counterpoints: Repairs could introduce semantic drift in typed relations.
RL training cost and benchmark coverage are unknown.
interpretation: A non-learned probe/diagnose/repair loop is a cheaper first test of the same idea inside World0's reflect() pipeline.

title: Retrieval-Driven Memory Reconsolidation for Long-Term LLM Agents (REALM)
thesis: Organize memories into a heterogeneous cognitive graph and revise them from retrieval feedback.
mechanism: Heterogeneous cognitive graph; reconsolidation triggered by retrieval outcomes.
implications: Retrieval/projection feedback as a signal for relation weight updates.

title: Governing Evolving Memory in LLM Agents: Risks, Mechanisms, and the Stability and Safety Governed Memory (SSGM) Framework
thesis: Evolving agent memory needs governance; consolidation should be a write-validation step guarding against logical drift.
mechanism: Governed memory framework with validation on consolidation writes.
implications: Validation gate for concept-card and relation writes by LLMs (concept integrity, priority 1 in AGENTS.md).

title: SCM: Sleep-Consolidated Memory with Algorithmic Forgetting for Large Language Models
thesis: Combine working-memory limits, NREM/REM-style phases, intentional forgetting and a computational self-model for introspection.
mechanism: Sleep-phase consolidation plus adaptive forgetting plus self-model.
evidence: Search summary reports perfect recall over ten-turn conversations and 90.9% memory-noise reduction on an eight-test suite (prototype scale; not independently checked).
limitations: Small-scale prototype per summary; not read.
implications: Only found paper pairing a self-model with offline consolidation; evidence weak.

title: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories
thesis: Parametric consolidation: Knowledge Seeding then a RL-driven 'Dreaming' phase generating synthetic rehearsal curricula.
limitations: Parametric, outside World0 scope (conceptual structure, not weights).
implications: Low direct relevance; useful as contrast.
